concepts.title: Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO)
concepts.one_liner: The Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) is a lower-bound on the data log-likelihood that serves as the objective function for Variational Autoencoders.
concepts.content: The VAE objective, $J$, is often called the **Evidence Lower Bound** or **ELBO**, because it is a lower-bound on the data log-likelihood (i.e. $J_p$, which equals $\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$). Using the definition of KL-divergence, we can rewrite $J$ as follows: $$\begin{aligned} J &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}) \Big] - \mathrm{KL}\left(q_\psi(Z \mid \mathbf{x}) \| p_{\mathbf{z}}\right) \end{aligned}$$ In this form, the VAE objective is presented as the sum of two terms. The first term measures the data log likelihood when the latent variables are sampled from $q_{\psi}$ and the second term measures the gap between $q_{\psi}$ and the distribution of latent variables, $p_{\mathbf{z}}$, which we actually should have been sampling from to obtain the correct estimate of $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$.
concepts.motivation_md: Directly maximizing the data log-likelihood in latent variable models is often computationally intractable. The ELBO provides a surrogate objective that is easier to optimize while ensuring that maximizing it also improves the true likelihood.
concepts.recap_md: - The ELBO is a lower bound on the log-likelihood of the observed data.

concepts.title: Connection between VAEs and Autoencoders
concepts.one_liner: VAEs function like stochastic autoencoders where the objective includes a reconstruction error term and a KL divergence term to regularize the latent space.
concepts.content: Variational Autoencoders make use of both an encoder $f_{\psi}$ (which parameterizes $q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})$) and a decoder $g_{\theta}$ (which parameterizes $p_{\theta}(X \bigm | \mathbf{z})$). For a simple VAE on one-dimensional data, we define the means and variances of the Gaussians: $$\begin{aligned} \mu_z &= f^{\mu}_{\psi}(x), & \sigma^2_z &= f^{\Sigma}_{\psi}(x)\\ \mu_x &= g^{\mu}_{\theta}(z), & \sigma^2_x &= g^{\Sigma}_{\theta}(z) \end{aligned}$$ The VAE learning problem seeks to maximize the following objective: $$\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \Big( \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{z\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | x^{(i)})}\Big[ \log p_{\theta}(x^{(i)} \bigm | z) \Big]}_{\text{likelihood term}} - \underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\left(q_\psi\left(Z \mid x^{(i)}\right) \| p_z\right)}_{\text{KL term}} \Big) \end{aligned}$$ For each datapoint $x$, the KL term can be computed in closed form: $$\mathrm{KL}\left(q_\psi(Z \mid x) \| p_z\right) = \frac{1}{2}(\mu_z^2 + \sigma_z^2 - \log(\sigma_z^2) - 1)$$. The likelihood term is approximated by sampling a single $z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_z, \sigma^2_z)$ and measuring the probability the decoder places on the input: $$\begin{aligned} \log p_{\theta}(x | z) &= \log\frac{1}{\sigma_x\sqrt{2\pi}} - \frac{(x - \mu_x)^2}{2\sigma_x^2} \end{aligned}$$ This process of encoding, sampling, and decoding to measure reconstruction error mirrors an autoencoder. (see figure: To evaluate the likelihood a VAE places on a datapoint $x$, we encode $x$ into $z$-space and then decode back and compute the reconstruction error. This corresponds to one importance sample for...) The differences are that we sample a stochastic $z$, the reconstruction error is scaled by predicted variance, and we add a KL loss term. The full objective is: $$\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \Big( \log\frac{1}{\sigma_{x^{(i)}}\sqrt{2\pi}} - \frac{(x^{(i)} - \mu_{x^{(i)}})^2}{2\sigma_{x^{(i)}}^2} - \frac{1}{2}(\mu_{z^{(i)}}^2 + \sigma_{z^{(i)}}^2 - \log(\sigma_{z^{(i)}}^2) - 1) \Big)$$
concepts.motivation_md: By framing generative modeling as an autoencoding task, VAEs can leverage neural networks to learn efficient latent representations while maintaining a probabilistic framework for data generation.
concepts.recap_md: - VAEs use an encoder to parameterize a latent distribution and a decoder to reconstruct the input.

The only differences from an autoencoder are that 1) we sample a stochastic $z$ from the output of the encoder, 2) the reconstruction error is scaled and offset by the predicted variance of the Gaussian likelihood model, and 3) we add to this term the KL loss defined previously.

concepts.title: Reconstruction Error
concepts.one_liner: Reconstruction error measures the discrepancy between the original input and the output of the decoder in an autoencoding architecture.
concepts.content: In the context of a VAE, the reconstruction error is a component of the log-likelihood measurement: $$\begin{aligned} \mu_x, \sigma^2_x &= g_{\theta}(z) & \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{Decode $z$}&\\ \log p_{\theta}(x | z) &= \log \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_x, \sigma^2_x) &\\ &= \log\frac{1}{\sigma_x\sqrt{2\pi}} - \frac{\overbrace{(x - \mu_x)^2}^{\text{reconstruction error}}}{2\sigma_x^2} & \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{Measure likelihood} \end{aligned}$$ This term quantifies how well the model can recreate the original input $x$ from the latent representation $z$.
concepts.motivation_md: To learn a useful representation, the model must be able to recover the original data from its compressed form; reconstruction error provides the signal to ensure information is preserved.
concepts.recap_md: - It is defined as the squared difference $(x - \mu_x)^2$ in a Gaussian likelihood model.

concepts.title: Reparameterization Trick
concepts.one_liner: The reparameterization trick allows backpropagation through stochastic nodes by expressing a random variable as a deterministic transformation of a fixed noise source.
concepts.content: To train a VAE, we need to backpropagate through the sampling step $z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_z, \sigma^2_z)$. The **reparameterization trick** sidesteps the difficulty of backpropagating through a stochastic function by reparameterizing the sample as: $$\begin{aligned} \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\\ z = \mu_z + \epsilon \sigma_z \end{aligned}$$ This makes $z$ a deterministic transformation of a fixed noise source $\epsilon$. To optimize the encoder, we only need to backpropagate through $\mu_z$ and $\sigma_z$, which are deterministic functions of $x$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard backpropagation cannot pass through random sampling operations. This trick makes the stochasticity an external input, allowing gradients to flow to the parameters of the distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - It transforms a stochastic sampling process into a differentiable deterministic function.

key_passage.text: This step is known as the reparameterization trick, as it reparameterizes a stochastic function (sampling from a Gaussian parameterized by a neural net) to be a deterministic transformation of a fixed noise source (the unit Gaussian).

concepts.title: Tension between KL Term and Reconstruction Error
concepts.one_liner: The VAE works through a tension between the KL term, which squashes latents toward the origin, and the reconstruction error, which spreads them out to preserve information.
concepts.content: The KL term encourages the encodings $z^{(i)}$ to be near a unit Gaussian distribution. If we fix $\sigma_{z^{(i)}}$ to 1, the KL term reduces to $\frac{1}{2}(\mu_{z^{(i)}}^2 - 1) \propto \mu_{z^{(i)}}^2$, which encourages the encodings $\mu_{z^{(i)}}$ to be as close to zero as possible, squashing the distribution of latents toward the origin. Minimizing the reconstruction error, conversely, requires that the latents do not collapse; it wants them to be spread out to preserve information about the inputs $x^{(i)}$. The tension between these two terms causes the VAE to produce a tightly packed latent space that can be densely sampled from, unlike standard autoencoders which may have gaps in their latent space. (see figure: Training a VAE to model the blue distribution. The Gaussian components spread out to tile both the embedding space and the data space.)
concepts.motivation_md: Without this tension, the latent space might become disorganized or overfit to specific training points. The KL term acts as a regularizer that ensures the latent space follows a predictable distribution suitable for generation.

concepts.title: VAEs for Representation Learning
concepts.one_liner: VAEs learn compressed embeddings that map data to a low-dimensional latent code while potentially encouraging desirable properties like disentanglement.
concepts.content: While VAEs are often viewed as generative models, the encoder can be useful as an end in itself for representation learning. Like standard autoencoders, the VAE encoder maps data to a low-dimensional latent code that preserves information about the input. VAEs may go beyond autoencoders because the embeddings can have other desirable properties depending on the prior $p_{\mathbf{z}}$. For example, using a unit Gaussian prior $p_{\mathbf{z}} = \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ encourages the dimensions of the embedding to be independent, a property called **disentanglement**.
concepts.motivation_md: Learning a compact, structured representation of data is essential for downstream tasks like classification, visualization, or controlled data generation.
concepts.recap_md: - VAE encoders provide compressed embeddings similar to standard autoencoders.

key_passage.text: Not only do VAEs learn a compressed embedding, the embeddings may also have other desirable properties depending on the prior p_z. For example, if p_z = N(0,1), as is common, then the loss encourages that the dimensions of the embedding are independent, a property called disentanglement.

concepts.title: Disentanglement
concepts.one_liner: Disentanglement is a property where individual dimensions of a latent embedding correspond to independent factors of variation in the data.
concepts.content: In representation learning, if the prior $p_{\mathbf{z}} = \mathcal{N}(0,1)$, the loss encourages the dimensions of the embedding to be independent, a property called **disentanglement**. Disentanglement means that we can vary one dimension of the embedding at a time, and just one independent factor of variation in the generated images will change. For example, one dimension might control the direction of light in a scene while another dimension controls the intensity of light.
concepts.motivation_md: Disentangled representations are more interpretable and allow for more precise control when generating or manipulating data.
concepts.recap_md: - It allows independent control over specific features of the generated output.

concepts.title: Nonidentifiability
concepts.one_liner: Nonidentifiability refers to the situation where multiple sets of parameters or mechanisms can equivalently explain the observed data.
concepts.content: It is important to realize that VAEs, and most representation learning methods, do not necessarily recover the true causal mechanisms that generated the data. Instead, they might find other mechanisms that can equivalently explain the data. A formal name for this issue is the **nonidentifiability** of the true parameters that generated a dataset.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding nonidentifiability is crucial for interpreting learned models, as it warns that the discovered latent factors may not correspond to the actual physical or causal processes of the real world.
concepts.recap_md: - It means different parameter settings can produce the same observed data distribution.

concepts.title: GANs as Representation Learners

position.section_title: Generative Adversarial Networks Are Representation Learners Too

concepts.one_liner: Generative Adversarial Networks, like VAEs, can learn meaningful and disentangled latent representations by mapping low-dimensional variables to high-dimensional data.
concepts.content:
Generative adversarial networks (GANs) train a mapping from latent variables to synthesized data, $g: \mathbf{z} \rightarrow \mathbf{y}$. Like Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), GANs can learn meaningful and disentangled latent representations. For example, a BigGAN trained on ImageNet can discover latent variables that independently control features such as background color and a bird's orientation.

(see figure: Walking in in two orthogonal directions in BigGAN @brock2018large)

This capability stems from the structural similarity between a GAN generator and a VAE decoder: both map a low-dimensional random variable $\mathbf{z}$ (typically $p_{\mathbf{z}} = \mathcal{N}(0,1)$) to data. Because the dimensions of $\mathbf{z}$ are a priori independent, and the goal is to create synthetic data with the properties of real data, these models naturally learn useful representations. GANs and VAEs are part of a larger class of models that map simple, high-entropy distributions to more structured, low-entropy distributions.
concepts.motivation_md: While GANs are primarily known for generating realistic images, it is important to understand if they also organize information internally. This concept explains that GANs, like VAEs, naturally learn disentangled representations because of their architecture, making them useful for representation learning tasks beyond simple generation.
concepts.recap_md: - GANs learn to map independent latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ to structured data $\mathbf{y}$.

key_passage.text: In both cases, they map a low-dimensional random variable z to data, and typically p_z = N(0,1). That means that the dimensions of z are a priori independent (disentangled). In both models the goal is roughly the same: create synthetic data that has all the properties of real data.

concepts.title: The Relationship between Generative Modeling and Representation Learning
concepts.one_liner: Generative modeling and representation learning are essentially inverse problems, mapping between raw data and simple underlying embeddings.
concepts.content:
Generative modeling and representation learning are closely related fields that learn mappings both to and from data. Generative models map a simple base distribution (noise) to data, while representation learning maps data to simple underlying representations called embeddings. These two problems are essentially inverses of each other, and solving one can often inform the solution to the other.

In deep learning, neural networks can be viewed from two perspectives. Moving from raw data to abstracted representations layer-by-layer highlights representation learning. Conversely, moving backward from abstracted representations to concrete data highlights generative modeling. Both directions are valid and form a full picture of the relationship between data and embeddings.

(see figure: The relationship between representation learning and generative modeling. Here we label one side as "Data" and the other as "Embedding"; but what's the precise difference between these two things?...)

While backpropagation also moves backward through a network, it computes the gradient $\nabla f$, whereas generative modeling focuses on the inverse function $f^{-1}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the symmetry between generation and representation allows researchers to build models that not only create realistic data but also understand the underlying structure of that data, leading to more robust and interpretable AI.
concepts.recap_md: - Generative models map noise to data; representation learning maps data to embeddings.

slots.example:
Generative modeling and representation learning are closely related fields that learn mappings both to and from data. Generative models map a simple base distribution (noise) to data, while representation learning maps data to simple underlying representations called embeddings. These two problems are essentially inverses of each other, and solving one can often inform the solution to the other.

In deep learning, neural networks can be viewed from two perspectives. Moving from raw data to abstracted representations layer-by-layer highlights representation learning. Conversely, moving backward from abstracted representations to concrete data highlights generative modeling. Both directions are valid and form a full picture of the relationship between data and embeddings.

(see figure: The relationship between representation learning and generative modeling. Here we label one side as "Data" and the other as "Embedding"; but what's the precise difference between these two things?...)

While backpropagation also moves backward through a network, it computes the gradient $\nabla f$, whereas generative modeling focuses on the inverse function $f^{-1}$.

concepts.title: Latent Variables as Representations
concepts.one_liner: Latent variables in generative models serve as complete representations of the data, capturing all unobserved factors that affect the output.
concepts.content: In generative models, latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ specify all unobserved factors that affect the model's output. For example, in a model predicting the color of a black and white photo ($g: \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z} \rightarrow \mathbf{y}$), $\mathbf{x}$ is the input image and $\mathbf{z}$ represents information that cannot be inferred from the input alone, such as the specific color of a shirt. In unconditional generative models, latent variables act as a complete representation of the data, meaning all information in the generated data is controlled by and represented within these variables.
concepts.motivation_md: Latent variables allow models to handle ambiguity and variety. By treating these variables as representations, we can manipulate specific features of generated data by simply changing the underlying latent code.
concepts.recap_md: - Latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ represent unobserved factors or features of the data.

concepts.title: Marginal Likelihood
concepts.one_liner: The marginal likelihood is the probability of the data under a model, calculated by integrating over all unobserved latent variables.
concepts.content:
The data log likelihood function $L(\{\mathbf{x}\}_{i=1}^N, \theta)$ measures the log likelihood of the data under a model $p_{\theta}$:

$$\begin{aligned} L(\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N, \theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}) \end{aligned}$$

To compute $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$, we can express it as the marginal likelihood, which marginalizes over all unobserved latent variables $\mathbf{z}$:

$$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})d\mathbf{z} \end{aligned}$$

This approach reduces the modeling problem to learning the conditional distribution $p_{\theta}(X \bigm | \mathbf{z})$, assuming $p_{\mathbf{z}}$ is known. For instance, the conditional distribution can be modeled as a unit Gaussian centered on the output of a function $g(\mathbf{z})$, such that $p_{\theta}(X \bigm | \mathbf{z}) = \mathcal{N}(\mu = g(\mathbf{z}), \sigma = \mathbf{1})$.
concepts.motivation_md: In models with hidden factors, we cannot observe the latent variables directly. Marginal likelihood allows us to evaluate how well our model fits the observed data by accounting for all possible states of those hidden factors.
concepts.recap_md: - Marginal likelihood integrates the conditional probability $p(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{z})$ over the distribution of latent variables $p(\mathbf{z})$.

concepts.title: Variational Autoencoder (VAE)
concepts.one_liner: A Variational Autoencoder (VAE) turns a standard autoencoder into a generative model by regularizing the latent space and adding noise to the encoder.
concepts.content:
A variational autoencoder (VAE) is a model that transforms an autoencoder into a generative model capable of synthesizing data. In a standard autoencoder, the decoder maps a representation $\mathbf{z}$ back to the data $\mathbf{x}$, functioning much like a generator.

(see figure: The relationship between an autoencoder and a generative model.)

However, a standard autoencoder does not provide a distribution $p_{\mathbf{z}}$ for sampling new images. Sampling a random $\mathbf{z}$ (e.g., from a unit Gaussian) might result in out-of-distribution inputs that the decoder cannot map to natural-looking images. The latent space of a vanilla autoencoder can be as complex as the data space itself.

(see figure: The latent space of an autoencoder can be just as complex as the data space.)

VAEs solve this by regularizing the latent distribution to fit a base distribution (like a Gaussian) and adding noise to the encoder's output. This ensures the model maximizes data likelihood under a formal probabilistic framework and allows for effective sampling.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard autoencoders are good for compression but bad for generation because their latent spaces are often disjointed. VAEs enforce a continuous, smooth latent space, making it possible to sample new, realistic data points.
concepts.recap_md: - VAEs regularize the latent space into a standard distribution to enable data synthesis.

The trick is very simple: just take a vanilla autoencoder and (1) regularize the latent distribution to squish it into a Gaussian (or some other base distribution), (2) add noise to the output of the encoder.

concepts.title: Mixture of Gaussians
concepts.one_liner: A mixture of Gaussians is a classical model that represents a density as a weighted sum of Gaussian distributions.
concepts.content:
VAEs are mixture models, and the most common kind of VAE is a mixture of Gaussians. The mixture of Gaussians model is a classical model that represents a density as a weighted sum of Gaussian distributions:

$$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^k w_i \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{\mu}_i, \mathbf{\Sigma}_i) \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{mixture of Gaussians} \end{aligned}$$

where the parameters are $\theta = \{\mathbf{\mu}_i, \mathbf{\Sigma}_i\}_{i=1}^k$, representing the mean and variance of all Gaussians in the mixture.
concepts.motivation_md: Mixture models allow for the representation of complex, multi-modal data distributions by combining several simpler distributions (like Gaussians), providing more flexibility than a single distribution.

concepts.title: Infinite Mixture of Gaussians
concepts.one_liner: An infinite mixture of Gaussians models a distribution by integrating over a continuous set of Gaussian components parameterized by a function.
concepts.content:
Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) use an infinite mixture of Gaussians, where the number of components $k \rightarrow \infty$. To parameterize an infinite mixture, the mean and variance are treated as functions of an underlying continuous variable $\mathbf{z}$. You can think of a function as the infinite set of values a variable takes on over some domain.

The function used by the VAE is $g_{\theta}$, decomposed into $g_{\theta}^{\mu}$ and $g_{\theta}^{\Sigma}$ to separately model the means and variances. By choosing a unit Gaussian distribution as the continuous domain to integrate over, the infinite mixture is described as:

$$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} \underbrace{\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}; g^{\mu}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}), g^{\Sigma}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}))}_{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} | \mathbf{z})}\underbrace{\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{z}; \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})}_{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}d\mathbf{z} \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{VAE hypothesis space} \end{aligned}$$

This models an infinite mixture as an integral that marginalizes over a continuous latent variable. This can be viewed as transforming a base distribution $p_{\mathbf{z}}$ to a modeled distribution $p_{\theta}$ by applying a deterministic mapping $g_{\theta}$ and adding Gaussian probability around each point in the range.

(see figure: From a finite mixture of Gaussians to an infinite mixture.)

While this example uses Gaussians, VAEs can be constructed using other base distributions, making mixture models metamodels whose components can be any density model.
concepts.motivation_md: Finite mixtures are limited by a fixed number of components; infinite mixtures provide a more powerful "metamodel" capable of representing highly complex data by marginalizing over a continuous latent space.
concepts.recap_md: - Extends Gaussian mixtures to the limit where the number of components $k$ approaches infinity.

concepts.title: The Challenge of Optimizing VAEs
concepts.one_liner: The VAE objective is intractable because its exact computation requires integrating over an infinite set of deep network forward passes.
concepts.content:
The VAE's objective is intractable because its exact computation requires integrating over an infinite set of deep net forward passes. The difficulty of optimizing VAEs lies in approximating this intractable objective. Once an approximation is derived, optimization can be performed using backpropagation on the approximate loss.

With the objective and hypothesis given, the VAE learning problem is defined as:

$$\begin{aligned} \theta^* &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\theta} L(\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N, \theta)\\ &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^N \log \int_{\mathbf{z}} \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}; g^{\mu}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}), g^{\Sigma}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})) \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{z}; \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})d\mathbf{z} \end{aligned}$$

where the integral represents the marginal likelihood $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard deep learning optimization requires a computable gradient; since the VAE marginal likelihood involves an intractable integral, we must find ways to approximate it to enable training.

concepts.title: Monte Carlo Estimation of the VAE Objective
concepts.one_liner: Monte Carlo estimation approximates the intractable VAE likelihood integral by averaging the likelihood over a finite set of random latent samples.
concepts.content:
Because the integral for $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})$ may not have a closed form for complex functions $g_{\theta}$, it must be approximated numerically. A Monte Carlo estimate approximates the integral as an expectation over the latent distribution:

$$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) &= \int_{\mathbf{z}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})d\mathbf{z}\\ &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}[p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})]\\ &\approx \frac{1}{M} \sum_{j=1}^M p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}^{(j)}), \quad \mathbf{z}^{(j)} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}} \end{aligned}$$

This allows the learning problem to be written in a closed differentiable form. In practice, for each iteration of backpropagation, a batch of random samples $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}$ is collected from the training set and a batch of random latents $\{\mathbf{z}^{(j)}\}$ is sampled from the unit Gaussian. Each $\mathbf{z}$ is passed through the network $g_{\theta}$ to evaluate the log probabilities of the $\mathbf{x}$ samples, followed by a backward pass to update parameters $\theta$.

(see figure: Fitting an infinite mixture of Gaussians whose means and variances are parameterized by a generator function $g_\theta$)

concepts.title: Importance Sampling
concepts.one_liner: Importance sampling is a technique for approximating expectations by sampling from a biased distribution and applying a correction factor.
concepts.content:
Monte Carlo estimation does not scale well to high dimensions because many samples from $p_{\mathbf{z}}$ are needed to accurately estimate the integral. In a VAE, most terms $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} | \mathbf{z}^{(j)})$ are near zero because a datapoint $\mathbf{x}$ only has substantial probability under Gaussians whose means are near $\mathbf{x}$.

(see figure: To estimate $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$ we only need to consider the Gaussian components (gray circles) that place significant probability on $\mathbf{x}$.)

Importance sampling addresses this by sampling from a different density $q_{\mathbf{z}}$ that focuses on regions where $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} | \mathbf{z})$ is large, then multiplying by a correction factor $\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}$:

$$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} q_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}) d\mathbf{z} = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\mathbf{z}}}\Big[\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})\Big] \end{aligned}$$

concepts.title: Variational Inference
concepts.one_liner: Variational inference approximates an intractable density by finding the closest tractable distribution within a parameterized family, typically by minimizing KL divergence.
concepts.content:
Variational inference is a strategy used to approximate an intractable density $p$ by finding the nearest density in a tractable family $q_{\psi}$. In VAEs, the ideal importance density $p_{\theta}(Z | \mathbf{x})$ is approximated by a Gaussian $q_{\psi} = \mathcal{N}(f_{\psi}^{\mu}(\mathbf{x}), f_{\psi}^{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x}))$, where $f_{\psi}$ acts as a probabilistic encoder.

(see figure: A VAE's encoder, $f_{\psi}$, models $p(Z \| \mathbf{x})$ as a Gaussian parameterized by $f_{\psi}(\mathbf{x})$.)

The goal is to choose $q_{\psi}$ to minimize the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence to the true posterior. This leads to the maximization of the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), denoted as $J$:

$$\begin{aligned} J = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}) \Big] - \mathrm{KL}\left(q_\psi(Z \mid \mathbf{x}) \| p_{\mathbf{z}}\right) \end{aligned}$$

This objective $J$ is a lower-bound on the data log-likelihood $J_p = \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$. By maximizing $J$, we simultaneously optimize the model parameters $\theta$ and the variational parameters $\psi$. The first term of the ELBO measures the reconstruction likelihood, while the second term measures the gap between the approximate posterior and the prior.
concepts.motivation_md: The true posterior distribution in complex models is often impossible to compute; variational inference turns this estimation problem into an optimization problem that can be solved with gradient descent.
concepts.recap_md: - Approximates the posterior $p(Z|X)$ using a tractable distribution $q(Z|X)$.

concepts.title: Probabilistic Encoder
concepts.one_liner: A probabilistic encoder is a function that maps an input to the parameters of a probability distribution over a latent space.
concepts.content:
In VAEs, the ideal importance density $p_{\theta}(Z | \mathbf{x})$ is approximated with a tractable family $q_{\psi}$. The most common choice is a Gaussian conditioned on $\mathbf{x}$: $q_{\psi} = \mathcal{N}(f_{\psi}^{\mu}(\mathbf{x}), f_{\psi}^{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x}))$. The function $f_{\psi}$ maps from the input $\mathbf{x}$ to the parameters (mean and variance) of a distribution over the latent variable $\mathbf{z}$. This function $f_{\psi}$ is known as a probabilistic encoder.

(see figure: A VAE's encoder, $f_{\psi}$, models $p(Z \| \mathbf{x})$ as a Gaussian parameterized by $f_{\psi}(\mathbf{x})$.)

In the VAE architecture, $f$ plays the role of the encoder while the generator function $g$ plays the role of the decoder.

concepts.title: Jensen's Inequality
concepts.one_liner: Jensen's inequality is used in VAEs to establish that the ELBO is a lower bound on the marginal log-likelihood.
concepts.content:
Jensen's inequality is used to show that the VAE objective $J$ is a lower-bound on the data log-likelihood $J_p = \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$:

$$\begin{aligned} J_p &= \log \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x})} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})\Big]\\ &\geq \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[\log \big(\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x})} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})\big)\Big] \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{Jensen's inequality}\\ &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[-\log q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) + \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}) + \log p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z}) \Big]\\ &= J \quad\quad\triangleleft\quad\text{VAE objective}\\ &\Rightarrow \quad J \leq J_p \end{aligned}$$

This inequality allows us to maximize a tractable expectation $J$ instead of the intractable log-likelihood $J_p$.
concepts.motivation_md: Jensen's inequality provides the mathematical justification for replacing a difficult 'log of an expectation' with a simpler 'expectation of a log', which is essential for deriving the ELBO in variational inference.
concepts.recap_md: - Proves that $\log \mathbb{E}[f(z)] \geq \mathbb{E}[\log f(z)]$ for positive functions.
